g.passage: We never reached the far wall that summer, though Dario spoke of it each morning as if distance were only another word to learn. He sat on the rim of the salt pool in Havana, trousers rolled, and named things in the language of his village: tile, gull, the green rust on the ladder. Bartolo repeated each word and swam a length before the next. On Thursday she stopped short of the far wall, held the rope, and came back saying she had only wanted to rest. Dario nodded and gave her the word for rest, then a second, older word that he said meant resting before one has finished. She practiced it without asking why. Later, reciting the colors, he paused at the word for the rust, and let her supply it, which she did loudly, as though he had been testing her. On the walk home she carried his towel over her shoulder, still damp at one corner where the rope had dripped on it.

g.passage: “Read me the one in the blue envelope, Cleotilde,” Ofelia said, before I had even set the brake on her chair. Each night that month I had wheeled her along the promenade at Valparaiso, and each night she had me stop at the same bench, facing the harbor where her son's ship had sailed in March, though she never once mentioned the ship. That afternoon, changing her pillow, I had found the envelope addressed to him, unstamped, its flap worn soft from being opened. When I asked whether she wished me to post it, she asked instead whether the gulls had been louder this year. I said I thought not. So I read it to her under the lamp, and she listened with her eyes on the water, correcting me twice where I had softened a word she had written harshly. When I finished, she had me fold it along its old creases and tuck it back beneath her blanket.

g.passage: Haruto rises when you come into the tailor's back room in Addis Ababa, which he has never once done in nine years, and offers you the better chair. You take the stool by the bolts of cotton instead and thank him warmly. The two of you bake on the same street; the old rule, written down by no one, says that he keeps the mornings for bread and you keep the afternoons for cake. Now the tailor wants a wedding loaf by Friday, and whoever bakes it will have either broken the rule or proven it still holds. Haruto asks after your mother. You ask after his oven, the one that cracked in May, and he says it is mended, mended very well. The tailor measures a sleeve and does not look up. When she finally names a price, you both say at once that the other should have it, and then neither of you reaches for the order slip lying between you, curling a little in the heat.

g.passage: Years later, Larissa would call that week a matter of logistics. The guesthouse beside the old monastery in Lisbon had been sold, and she and Caio, who had shared its thin middle wall for twenty years, were the last to clear their rooms. She labeled her boxes by weight, not by contents. She rented the van for the shortest day the company offered. When Caio knocked to ask whether she wanted the wall clock, the one whose ticking had reached both their beds, she said it would only need a new battery and that he should keep it. By Thursday both rooms were bare except for that clock, which neither of them had taken down. She checked the windows twice, signed the key form in the porter's office, and went back upstairs because, she told the porter, she thought she had left a pen. The clock was still on the wall, and she stood a while with her hand flat against the plaster beside it.
g.question: Which choice best describes the overall tone of the passage?

g.passage: Would the call come before the bus reached Central Avenue? Waya kept turning his phone face down on his knee and then face up again. Beside him, Kamal sat with the toolbag across his lap, its canvas patched so often that the original color survived only under the straps. The bid for the church restoration had gone in a month ago; if it was accepted, Waya would cut his first joints on a job that mattered, and Kamal would have one more winter of work before his hands gave out. All evening the old man had talked about grain instead, how oak lies to you and pine tells the truth too fast. But when the bus lurched, Waya noticed that Kamal's thumb had been running along the same seam for miles, as if it were a board that would not come true, worrying a pale groove into the cloth. g.passage: Three rules governed the galley of the training ship docked at Manila that summer: knives point down, nothing left on the burners, and no one cries where the cook can see. Neema from the city office with a rolled survey,
and for an hour they practiced polite English,
would you, could you, may I,
laughing when the verbs came out crooked.
Neema drew the new road in chalk across the board,
a straight white line through the hills,
and said, Would you come see the plans in the city?
Thida said, Thank you, I could not,
each word placed exactly where the lesson had put it.
They finished the page on conditionals.
Neema rubbed the road off with her sleeve,
and the chalk dust settled on the map between them.
g.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?
options: From formal unease to a growing, relaxed warmth between the two
From playful confusion over verbs to proud mastery of the lesson
From bright hope about the road to open anger at its chosen route
From easy shared laughter to a correct, carefully distanced politeness
g.explanation: 앞부분에서 두 사람은 정중한 영어 표현을 연습하며 동사가 틀릴 때 함께 웃는다. Neema가 새 도로를 그리고 도시로 초대하자, Thida는 수업에서 배운 그대로 정확한 말로 거절하고, 이후 두 사람은 말없이 남은 연습만 끝낸다. 칠판의 도로를 지우고 분필 가루가 지도 위에 내려앉는 장면도 거리감을 남기므로 D가 정답이다. A는 변화 방향을 뒤집었고, B는 수업 내용만 보았으며, C는 드러나지 않은 분노를 과장했다.

seed.relationship: a grandson and the grandfather's old friend
seed.conflict: after a mistake that only one person noticed
seed.topicSeed: an apartment stairwell in Porto Alegre; a grandson and the grandfather's old friend after a mistake that only one person noticed

g.passage: After my grandfather's funeral in Porto Alegre, I volunteered to carry the folding chairs back up to the fourth floor, partly so I would be thanked on the way. I was Fausto, the grandson who had read the eulogy, and people squeezed my arm on every landing and told me how well I had captured him. Joaquim, his friend since their years on the docks, climbed behind me with two chairs of his own and said nothing until the third floor. There he mentioned, mildly, that my grandfather had never sailed to Recife; it was Joaquim who had gone, and my grandfather who had stayed to mind both their families. He said no one else would know. Then he asked me to take the chair from his left hand, which was shaking. We went up the last flight slowly, I in front, counting the steps aloud for him, the way my grandfather used to count them for me.
g.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?
options: From self-satisfied pride to a humbled, reflective attentiveness
From fresh grief over the death to gentle amusement at Joaquim
From quiet resentment of Joaquim to admiring thanks for his help
From proud confidence to deep shame expressed in an open apology
g.explanation: 처음에 Fausto는 칭찬을 받으려고 의자를 나르겠다고 나섰고, 계단마다 추도사를 칭찬받으며 자랑스러워한다. 3층에서 Joaquim이 추도사의 실수를 조용히 알려 주자, 그는 변명하지 않고 Joaquim의 의자를 받아 들고 할아버지가 하던 대로 계단을 세어 준다. 따라서 자기만족적 자부심에서 겸허하고 세심한 성찰로 바뀐다는 A가 정답이다. B와 C는 근거 없는 감정이고, D는 지문에 없는 공개적 사과로 과장했다.

seed.relationship: a violin student and an exacting teacher
seed.conflict: over whether to sell a shared inheritance
seed.topicSeed: a radio repair shop in Accra; a violin student and an exacting teacher over whether to sell a shared inheritance

g.passage: “Sell it,” Mehrnaz said, “and you sell the only thing he ever tuned for both of us.” Seoyeon did not answer. They stood in the radio repair shop off Oxford Street in Accra, where the technician had just lifted the back from the old valve set their late teacher had left to them jointly. Seoyeon had a buyer's offer folded in her violin case; her tuition was due in a week. The technician talked while he worked, about the set's German tubes and the dealer in Kumasi who had first sold it, and neither woman interrupted him. Inside, the tubes began to glow amber. When he switched it on, a highlife station crackled in, then a violin concerto from somewhere far off, faint and slightly flat. Both women leaned toward it. Seoyeon heard Mehrnaz hum the correction under her breath, and found herself humming it too, a half step behind.
g.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: A disagreement is raised, then replaced by a history of the radio's origins.
A dispute is introduced and resolved when the women agree to keep the radio.
A conflict is posed, left unresolved, and then complicated by a shared response.
A technician's account is given, then challenged by the two women's memories.
g.explanation: 글은 라디오를 팔지 말지에 대한 Mehrnaz의 말과 Seoyeon의 침묵, 등록금 사정으로 갈등을 먼저 제시한다. 중간에는 수리공의 이야기가 이어지는 동안 갈등이 해결되지 않은 채 미뤄지고, 끝에서는 두 사람이 음정이 어긋난 협주곡에 똑같이 반응해 함께 교정음을 흥얼거리며 결정이 더 복잡해진다. 따라서 C가 정답이다. A는 중간의 라디오 내력을 글의 중심으로 보았고, B는 지문에 없는 합의를 가정했으며, D는 두 사람이 수리공의 말을 끊지 않았다는 점과 맞지 않는다.
